sourceNotes: Seeded from AAM roleplay performance indicators and marketing cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: AAM event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the marketing cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: Under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act a fiber present at 5% or less of total weight may not be named on the label and must be shown as "other fiber" — unless it carries a clearly established functional significance at that level, which is why 2% spandex may be named for stretch but 3% silk may not.
terms.whyItMatters: A written-event judge who hands you a hangtag reading "96% cotton, 4% silk" expects you to catch that the silk cannot be called out; naming a decorative trace fiber is a mislabeling exposure on every unit shipped.

terms.definition: The FTC Care Labeling Rule requires reliable evidence in hand before a garment ships for every instruction and every warning printed on the label — one complete method that will not harm the garment, plus a warning for any ordinary procedure that would.
terms.whyItMatters: In a vendor-compliance roleplay the safe-sounding answer is to print "dry clean only" on everything; the rule says an untested instruction is itself a violation, so the correct move is to demand the mill's wash-test data before the PO is cut.

terms.definition: The 2010 statute that deleted the Fur Products Labeling Act's exemption for garments whose fur was worth $150 or less, so a $40 parka with a coyote-trimmed hood now needs the animal's English name and country of origin exactly like a full fur coat does.
terms.whyItMatters: Accessory and outerwear cases lean on the dead $150 threshold as a trap; a competitor who still applies it will clear a trimmed hood or a rabbit-lined glove that is in fact a labeling violation.

terms.definition: A plain-surface fabric whose flame spread time in the 16 CFR 1610 test is 3.5 seconds or longer, which is the only class that may legally be sold as wearing apparel; below 3.5 seconds the fabric is Class 3, rapid and intense burning, and is banned outright.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a lab report showing a sheer 3.1-second burn, the exam wants the shipment stopped rather than discounted — the number decides legality, not quality.

terms.definition: Sleepwear in sizes 9 months through 14 must self-extinguish in a vertical flame test, averaging no more than 7.0 inches of char with no single specimen burning its full 10-inch length; only tight-fitting garments inside the CPSC maximum-dimension tables, or infant sizes 9 months and under, escape the test.
terms.whyItMatters: A loose-fitting cotton pajama program is the classic case trap — it is legal as a "lounge set" and illegal as sleepwear, and the char measurement is what separates them.

terms.definition: Upper outerwear in sizes 2T through 12 may carry no hood or neck drawstring at all, and waist or bottom drawstrings on sizes 2T through 16 may not extend more than 3 inches outside the channel with the garment at full width, and must be bar-tacked so they cannot pull through.
terms.whyItMatters: CPSC treats a violating hoodie as a substantial product hazard, so a merchandising roleplay that proposes cinched hoods for a kids' program is asking you to name the recall risk, not the trend.

terms.definition: The certificate a domestic manufacturer or importer must issue for goods designed primarily for children 12 and under, based on third-party testing at a CPSC-accepted lab against the 100 ppm total lead limit in substrate, 90 ppm lead in surface coating, and 0.1% phthalate limits, and paired with a permanent tracking label.
terms.whyItMatters: A children's accessory buy fails compliance on the paperwork before it fails on the product; the exam expects you to price the lab testing and the tracking label into the first cost, not to discover them at the port.

terms.definition: Customs classifies a blended textile garment under whichever fiber predominates by weight, and the duty rate follows that classification — so a 60/40 cotton-polyester knit shirt enters as cotton while the same shirt at 45/55 enters as man-made fiber, roughly doubling the rate on an identical-looking garment.
terms.whyItMatters: A sourcing case that offers a "cheaper" 55% polyester blend is really testing whether you can compute the landed cost after the classification flips; the fabric saving is often smaller than the duty jump.

terms.definition: Garment measurement minus body measurement — the room a wearer needs to move, breathe and sit, typically 2 to 4 inches at the bust for a woven blouse — held separate from design ease, which is the extra fullness a silhouette adds on top of it.
terms.whyItMatters: Fit-complaint roleplays hand you a size chart and a garment spec; subtracting one from the other tells you whether the problem is a body-measurement error or an intended oversized cut.

terms.definition: The share of original cost recovered by liquidating leftover seasonal goods to a jobber or off-price chain — often 20 to 30 cents on the cost dollar — which is the benchmark any further in-store markdown has to beat before it is worth taking.
terms.whyItMatters: With 400 units at $18 cost, a jobber offer of $5 recovers $2,000; the exam wants that compared against a final markdown's net proceeds and its carrying cost, not an instinct that liquidation is failure.

terms.definition: The worst defect rate a lot may average and still be accepted, applied through a sampling plan rather than a full count — under ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 General Level II a 3,000-unit lot draws a 125-piece sample, and at 2.5 AQL it is accepted on 7 defects and rejected on 8.
terms.whyItMatters: A quality roleplay reports 9 defects in a 125-piece pull; the plan says reject the lot, and knowing that a single extra defect flips the decision is what separates a competitor from a guess.

terms.definition: The percentage of a cutting layout's total area actually covered by pattern pieces, with the rest lost as waste; since fabric is usually the largest single element of garment cost, lifting a marker from 82% to 86% cuts fabric consumption per unit by roughly 5%.
terms.whyItMatters: When a cost sheet has to come down a dollar and the factory will not move on labor, this is the lever an apparel case expects you to pull before you cheapen the fabric.

terms.definition: Clothing, textiles and the fibers in them bought with Department of Defense funds must be grown and processed entirely in the United States at every stage — fiber, yarn spinning, weaving or knitting, dyeing, finishing and sewing — with no de minimis foreign allowance, and the exception line sits at the simplified acquisition threshold rather than at a percentage.
terms.whyItMatters: A uniform-contract roleplay offers a mill quote with Turkish yarn woven domestically; under the FTC's "all or virtually all" test that could still be argued, and under this statute it disqualifies the bid outright, so the two standards have to be priced separately.

terms.definition: Since June 2022 any merchandise mined, produced or manufactured wholly or in part in Xinjiang, or by a listed entity, is presumed to be forced-labor goods and is barred at the border; cotton is a named priority sector, and rebutting the presumption takes clear and convincing evidence of the whole supply chain plus full responsiveness to CBP, not a supplier's signed affidavit.
terms.whyItMatters: A sourcing roleplay hands you a vendor who can document the sewing factory but not the ginner; "wholly or in part" means a traced yarn is the deliverable, and the detained container is measured in weeks of a nine-week selling season.

terms.definition: The National Gold and Silver Stamping Act lets a marked fineness run under nominal by only 3 parts per thousand on an article carrying no solder and 7 parts per thousand on a soldered one, so a piece stamped 14K (0.583 nominal) must assay at least 0.580 unsoldered and 0.576 with solder, and silver stamped sterling gets 4 and 10 parts per thousand against 0.925.
terms.whyItMatters: An assay report reading 0.578 on a soldered 14K chain passes and the same number on a seamless bangle is a mislabeled shipment; the exam wants the tolerance applied to the construction, not a judgment that both are close enough.

terms.definition: Under the FTC Jewelry Guides this word may be printed only on a sterling silver base coated with at least 10 karat gold laid at least 2.5 micrometres thick — where gold-filled instead demands a bonded layer weighing at least 1/20 of the metal in the article, and gold electroplate needs only 0.175 micrometres, roughly one fourteenth as much gold as vermeil.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a supplier's spec sheet showing a brass core with 3 micrometres of 14K, the correct call in a merchandising roleplay is that the thickness passes and the base metal does not, so the word cannot go on the tag at any price point.

terms.definition: Diamond prices are quoted per carat and the per-carat rate itself jumps at the weight breaks buyers ask for — 0.50, 0.90, 1.00, 1.50 — so a 0.99 stone at $6,000 per carat costs $5,940 while a 1.00 stone at $7,500 per carat costs $7,500, a 26% price increase for 1% more weight.
terms.whyItMatters: A jewelry selling roleplay wants you to move a customer to the shy weight: total price is weight times the per-carat rate, and doing that multiplication in the right order is what shows the $1,560 saving on a stone nobody can eyeball as smaller.

terms.definition: EU rules cap what leaches out of an item rather than what it contains: less than 0.5 micrograms per square centimetre per week for anything in prolonged skin contact, and less than 0.2 for a post inserted into a pierced ear, measured after a wear-and-corrosion simulation standing in for two years of use.
terms.whyItMatters: An earring that passes on day one and fails after simulated wear is the trap in an accessories sourcing case — the plating thickness, not the alloy's nickel percentage, is what has to be specified into the purchase order.

terms.definition: The fixed increment a pattern piece grows at each point of measure when it is stepped up or down from the sample size — a 1-inch bust grade in misses is only 1/4 inch on each quarter of the pattern, and it is split again among the grade points, which is why a size 14 can gain a full inch of bust while the shoulder and armhole barely move.
terms.whyItMatters: When a fit complaint says the largest sizes pull across the back, the answer in a product-development roleplay is that the grade distributed too little of the increment to the upper body, not that the whole size chart is wrong.

terms.definition: A bra cup letter is not a fixed volume, it is the difference between the bust and underbust measurement — one inch of difference is an A, four inches a D — so cup volume travels with the band, and moving down a band while moving up a letter (34C to 32D) holds the same cup while tightening the support.
terms.whyItMatters: A fitting-room roleplay hands you a customer whose 34C rides up in back; the sale is saved by computing the 32D rather than by fetching a different style, and the arithmetic is what the judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Chest measurement minus trouser waist in a nested tailored suit, standardized at 6 inches in the United States — a 42 jacket ships with a 36 trouser — while an athletic cut runs a drop of 7 or 8 and a portly block runs 4 or less.
terms.whyItMatters: A menswear customer who wears a 42 jacket and a 34 waist is a drop 8, so the exam answer is suit separates or an alteration allowance, not a different size jacket that will hang wrong in the shoulder.

terms.definition: The one-third-inch unit that English-language shoe sizes still step by, with a half size worth 1/6 inch — so the entire adult run from a 7 to a 12 spans only 1 2/3 inches of last length, and US and UK scales differ by a sixth of an inch of zero point rather than by any difference in the step.
terms.whyItMatters: A footwear roleplay where the customer insists on going up two full sizes for comfort is really offering 2/3 of an inch; the fix is width or last shape, and knowing the step size is what lets you say so with a number.

terms.definition: A measuring device reads two lengths, overall heel-to-toe and heel-to-ball arch length, and the shoe must be fitted to whichever reading is larger, because the shoe's flex point has to land on the ball joint — a foot reading 9 overall and 10 arch takes the 10 and is fitted forward with padding, never the 9.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the single most common footwear selling roleplay: the customer's toes have room in the smaller size and the shoe still creases across the instep, and the judge is waiting for the arch reading to be named as the deciding measurement.

terms.definition: US ring sizes are a linear scale on inside diameter: size 0 is 0.458 inch and every full size adds 0.032 inch, which is about 2.55 mm of circumference, so a size 6 measures 0.650 inch across and moving a customer two sizes up stretches the shank roughly 5 mm.
terms.whyItMatters: Sizing service quotes turn on this number — most shanks tolerate about two sizes of stretch before metal must be cut in, so an order to take a size 5 heirloom to a 9 is a rebuild quote, not a resize quote.

terms.definition: Cut dimensions are the finished specification divided by one minus the tested shrinkage, not the specification multiplied by it — a 30-inch finished body length in fabric shrinking 4% must be cut at 30 / 0.96 = 31.25 inches, where multiplying by 1.04 gives 31.2 and lands the garment short of tolerance on every unit.
terms.whyItMatters: A production case gives you an AATCC wash-test result and a finished spec and expects the cutting length back; "Sanforized" only promises the residual is held to 1% or less, which changes the divisor, not the method.

terms.definition: The per-colorway floor the mill's dye lot and the cutting table impose, which is a different constraint from the order-level minimum: a program with a 3,000-unit order minimum and a 600-unit MCQ per color supports at most five colorways, so adding a sixth either strands 600 units or forces the whole buy up to 3,600.
terms.whyItMatters: An assortment roleplay that asks for "one more color" is asking for 600 units of exposure; naming the two minimums separately is what turns a vague sourcing objection into a number the buyer can decide on.

terms.definition: A quote covering only the factory's labor and findings, with the brand buying and consigning the fabric, so it cannot be compared with a full-package quote until fabric is added at consumption — a $3.10 CMT plus 1.8 yards at $3.60 is $9.58, which loses to a $9.40 full-package price on the same garment.
terms.whyItMatters: Sourcing cases present the CMT number first because it always looks cheaper; the exam is testing whether you rebuild both quotes onto the same basis before recommending the factory.

terms.definition: Weight in grams of 9,000 metres of a yarn, a direct system where a bigger number means a thicker filament — 15 for bridal-sheer hosiery, 40 and up for opaque tights — and the inverse of the cotton count system, where a bigger number means a finer yarn because it counts 840-yard hanks to the pound.
terms.whyItMatters: A hosiery or activewear case that quotes 20 denier against 40s cotton count is quoting two scales running opposite directions; reading both correctly is what stops a competitor recommending the heavier fabric by mistake.

terms.definition: Areal weight of a fabric, and the number that prices a knit garment, because knit goods are bought by the kilogram rather than the yard — a tee using 1.2 square metres of 180 gsm jersey carries 216 grams of fabric, so a jump to 220 gsm adds 48 grams of purchased weight per unit before any labor changes.
terms.whyItMatters: When a costing exercise asks why a heavier tee costs more than the yardage suggests, the answer is that the knit is invoiced on weight; converting from ounces per square yard at 33.9 grams each is the arithmetic the exam expects.

terms.definition: A thickness measure, not a weight: one ounce equals 1/64 inch of hide, so an 8-to-9-ounce belt strap runs about 1/8 inch thick and a 2-to-3-ounce garment leather is about 1/24 inch — while shoe soles are quoted in irons instead, each iron being 1/48 inch.
terms.whyItMatters: A handbag or belt spec written in ounces is describing stiffness and structure; a case that asks whether a 3-ounce hide can carry hardware is answered by converting to inches, and the unit's name points the wrong way.

terms.definition: The failure mode where yarns pull away from a stitch line under load rather than the thread breaking, tested by pulling a sewn specimen until the seam opens a quarter inch, with woven apparel typically specified at a 25-pound-force minimum; the fix is a wider seam allowance or a tighter fabric construction, never a stronger thread.
terms.whyItMatters: A quality report showing a 19-pound result on a slippery satin is the classic case where the tempting answer is to change the thread; the exam wants the construction change, because the thread never failed.

terms.definition: Boxing unsold seasonal goods to bring back next year instead of marking them down now, which is only worth it when the season-over-season carrying cost — warehouse, handling and capital, commonly 20 to 25% of cost for twelve months — stays below the loss the final markdown would take, and only for goods whose styling will still read next year.
terms.whyItMatters: Holding 500 basic wool scarves at $9 cost for a year runs roughly $1,000 against a 60% markdown that gives up more than that, while the same math on a trend silhouette fails, so the disposition roleplay turns on fashion risk and the carrying rate together.

terms.definition: Divides a brand's sales by its %ACV coverage so brands with unequal shelf presence can be compared on equal footing: $2,000,000 on 40% ACV is $50,000 per point and beats $3,000,000 on 90% ACV at $33,333 per point, which says the smaller brand has earned more distribution rather than more advertising.
terms.whyItMatters: A marketing-plan defense that has to say where the next dollar goes is decided by which brand turns each point of coverage into the most volume; the exam version simply hands sales and coverage and asks for the per-point figure.

terms.definition: Completed goal actions divided by the visits or clicks that could have completed them — the denominator is sessions, never impressions — so 40 orders from 2,000 landing-page visits is 2% no matter how many people saw the ad that sent them.
terms.whyItMatters: The single most common analytics error on the marketing exam is dividing sales by impressions; an item that supplies impressions, clicks and orders together is checking which denominator the competitor reaches for.

terms.definition: Placing the product in the customer's hands for a free trial, test drive or home-approval period and letting possession persuade, because giving the item back later registers as a loss. A takeaway close works from the opposite direction, threatening to withdraw the offer or the model rather than handing it over.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail and automotive roleplays with a hesitant buyer reward a named trial-based close, and pairing it with the store's return policy shows you know the company's selling rules.

terms.definition: Fully loaded center cost — wages, benefits, technology and facilities — divided by contacts handled; $180,000 a month across 30,000 contacts is $6.00 each. A live phone contact typically runs several times the cost of a self-service session, and that spread, not the software licence, is the business case for deflection.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a chatbot or a help center has to set this figure against the deflected channel to justify the spend.

terms.definition: A purchase for which buyers accept no substitute and will pass closer outlets to reach one brand -- insistence, not preference; a shopping good is one buyers compare on price, quality, and style across several stores and will happily switch brands on to save money.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution questions follow from this classification: specialty goods justify exclusive distribution and few outlets, while shopping goods need enough outlets for comparison to happen.

terms.definition: The pretrial phase in which each side must turn over relevant evidence through interrogatories, requests for production, depositions and requests for admission — which is why most business disputes settle once the documents surface. It also creates a duty to preserve records the moment litigation is reasonably anticipated, so routine deletion schedules have to be suspended under a litigation hold.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-procedure roleplays about a document-retention policy hinge on the litigation hold this phase triggers.

terms.definition: Plots competing brands against two axes chosen from the attributes buyers actually use to tell brands apart — often price against perceived quality — using respondent ratings rather than the firm's own specifications, and adds an ideal point where the target segment says it wants a brand to sit; an empty region on the map is a positioning opportunity only when an ideal point falls inside it, otherwise it is empty because nobody wants that combination.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning roleplays that hand you competitor data are scored on naming the two axes and defending why buyers discriminate on them; competitors lose the point by mapping attributes only the company cares about.

terms.definition: Buffer units sized as a service-level z-value times the standard deviation of demand over lead time, held only to absorb variability — unlike cycle stock, which is the working quantity consumed between deliveries and would exist even with perfectly steady demand.
terms.whyItMatters: A supplier-reliability roleplay turns on this: raising the promised in-stock service level raises the buffer more than proportionally, so the judge wants the cost of that extra protection weighed against the cost of a stockout.

terms.definition: Splits output growth into three addends — the contribution of added capital, the contribution of added hours, and the residual left over. If output rises 4% while capital and labor together explain 2.5%, the remaining 1.5% is productivity growth, the only piece that raises income per worker permanently.
terms.whyItMatters: Productivity items ask a competitor to separate growth that came from hiring more people from growth that came from each worker producing more.

terms.definition: The organized collection and analysis of information about markets, customers, and rivals.
terms.whyItMatters: Research helps a business understand needs before choosing tactics.

terms.definition: Measurable population traits such as age, income, education, and location.
terms.whyItMatters: Demographics let a business tailor marketing to specific segments.

terms.definition: A persuasive structure adapted from Carl Rogers' therapy: open by restating the opposing position accurately enough that its holder would accept your summary, name the conditions under which it is valid, and only then introduce your own claim and the ground the two share. It deliberately withholds the thesis until the audience has been disarmed, which makes it the standard choice for a hostile listener and a poor choice for one who already agrees and wants the recommendation in the first line.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which the judge plays an angry supervisor or a customer who has already refused once is scored on this opening move rather than on a louder restatement of your case.

terms.definition: Government and industry rules governing ad claims, content, and disclosure.
terms.whyItMatters: Compliance protects consumers and shields a business from liability.

terms.definition: Sellers must re-scrub their calling lists against the federal registry at least every 31 days, and may reach a listed consumer only through an existing business relationship — 18 months after that person's last purchase, or 3 months after an inquiry — or with signed written permission. A list bought once and used for a year fails the scrub requirement no matter how it was sourced.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a purchase date and a call date and ask whether the relationship exemption still covers the call; a prospecting roleplay is scored on saying how often the list is cleaned.

terms.definition: Systems and strategies for managing customer data, interactions, and relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: CRM tracks preferences and delivers personalized service at scale.

terms.definition: Moves a new product through fixed stages separated by go/kill reviews with written criteria, so a project can die at any gate -- screening, business analysis, development, testing, launch; the long-standing planning ratio is roughly 7 serious ideas entering for every 1 commercial success.
terms.whyItMatters: Development roleplays ask what happens between an idea and a launch; the scoring point is that each gate can kill the project, not that the stages happen in order.

terms.definition: Two independently known brands appear together on one finished offering and both stake positioning risk on it — a Doritos Locos Taco — whereas in ingredient branding one brand is a component inside a host product and is advertised to end users to pull the host's sales, as with Intel Inside; the ingredient brand never owns the final purchase decision, while co-brands share it and share the damage if the partner stumbles.
terms.whyItMatters: Partnership roleplays ask what each side actually contributes and risks; naming which of the two structures is on the table is the first thing the judge listens for.

terms.definition: Fisher and Ury's method built on four rules — separate the people from the problem, focus on interests instead of stated positions, invent options for mutual gain before deciding anything, and insist on an objective standard for the outcome. A position is what a party demands; the interest is why they want it, and only the interest can usually be satisfied in more than one way.
terms.whyItMatters: Negotiation roleplays are scored on surfacing the reason behind a demand and offering two options that meet it, which positional haggling over one number cannot produce.

terms.definition: The ongoing expenses of running a business — labor, materials, utilities, maintenance.
terms.whyItMatters: Controlling operating costs is a lever competitors use to lift profit.

terms.definition: Fraction of checkable deposits a bank is barred from lending — mandated reserves ÷ deposits. At 10%, a $1,000 deposit locks up $100 and frees $900, and the ceiling on deposit creation is 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10; cutting the ratio to 5% doubles that ceiling without the central bank buying a single security.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate-fluctuation items ask how a change in this one fraction moves the amount of money in circulation, and the answer is the reciprocal.

terms.definition: Split the population into internally similar subgroups, then draw at random inside every one of them, usually allocating each subgroup a share of the sample equal to its share of the population (n_h = n x N_h/N); cluster sampling looks similar but randomly picks a few whole groups and skips the rest entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: A sampling-plan roleplay that requires each store region to be represented in proportion is solved with strata, and the judge listens for the proportional allocation, not just the word random.

terms.definition: Forecasts a new brand's settled share as cumulative penetration × repeat-purchase rate × buying-rate index — 40% × 25% × 1.2 = 12% share — so a launch that everybody tries and nobody buys twice collapses on the middle term no matter how large the trial figure looks in the panel data.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product forecast items give the three panel figures and expect the multiplied share; in a plan presentation the same arithmetic is what separates a trial problem, which advertising can fix, from a repeat problem, which only the product can.

terms.definition: A purchase credited to an ad that was served and seen but never clicked, counted only when it falls inside a fixed look-back window — commonly one day for display against 30 days for a click — which is why these totals overstate a campaign next to click-through conversions.
terms.whyItMatters: A results presentation where the platform's reported sales exceed the client's actual order count is this in action, and the competitor is expected to say which conversions were assumed rather than observed.

terms.definition: The total amount of tax a person or business legally owes to the government.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax liabilities affect take-home income and the real return on financial decisions.

terms.definition: Total pay a rep receives at exactly 100% of quota — base salary plus variable pay at plan, so a $60,000 base with $60,000 of commission at plan is $120,000 at a 50/50 pay mix. It is a plan figure and not a promise: only the base half is paid regardless of results, which is what separates it from a salary.
terms.whyItMatters: A recruiting roleplay that pitches a sales job is scored on explaining the split honestly, and quoting the total as if it were guaranteed is an ethical mark against you.

terms.definition: Closed cases a customer reopens divided by cases closed in the period — 60 of 1,200 is 5%. It is the audit on first contact resolution: an agent can inflate the resolution figure by closing tickets early, and this is the only metric that catches it, which is why the two are always reported as a pair.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-quality case, the competitor who pairs a resolution claim with this check shows the judge they know the headline metric can be gamed.

terms.definition: Portable, shorter-lived business goods bought routinely by middle managers and written off over a few years -- hand tools, laptops, forklifts; an installation is the major capital asset such as a plant or a production line, approved by top management on a multi-year capital budget.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business selling roleplays are scored on calling on the right buyer: the pair differs by who signs, so pitching an installation to a department manager is a scoring miss.

terms.definition: Weakening of a famous mark's distinctiveness through blurring, where an unrelated use erodes the one-to-one link between mark and source, or tarnishment, where a use ties it to something unsavory; under the U.S. Trademark Dilution Revision Act of 2006 the owner of a mark famous to the general consuming public can sue without showing any likelihood of confusion or proof of actual economic injury, which is what makes it broader than ordinary infringement.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding and business-law roleplays about a licensing or extension request turn on this doctrine; citing the no-confusion-required standard is the technical half of the answer.

terms.definition: Average inventory divided by cost of goods sold, multiplied by 365 — the same relationship as inventory turnover but expressed as days on hand, so it falls when turnover rises and 365 divided by turnover reproduces it.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a balance sheet and a cost of goods sold figure, exam questions ask how long a firm's stock sits before selling; answering with the turnover ratio when the item asked for days is a scored miss.

terms.definition: Offers accepted divided by offers extended, times 100 — 27 acceptances on 36 offers is 75%. Declines by candidates who never received a formal offer are excluded, so the figure isolates whether pay and the closing conversation are competitive, not whether sourcing produced enough applicants.
terms.whyItMatters: In a compensation roleplay, a falling acceptance rate is the evidence that a pay range lags the market; the judge wants the ratio, not an impression that candidates seem unhappy.

terms.definition: Sum of the market shares of the four biggest sellers: 18 + 15 + 9 + 6 = 48%. Crossing roughly 40% marks an industry as an oligopoly, and 100% is a monopoly or a tight cartel — but because it adds shares without squaring them, it cannot tell four equal firms apart from one giant and three minnows.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition questions give a share table and ask for the structure label plus its threshold, and the blind spot is exactly what the follow-up tests.

terms.definition: Original data collected firsthand through surveys, interviews, or experiments.
terms.whyItMatters: It gives firsthand customer and market insight for a specific question.

terms.definition: Multiplies target households × awareness % × trial % × availability (%ACV) × repeat % × units bought per repeat buyer to reach a first-year volume, so a chain of five decimals well below 1.0 shrinks 10,000,000 households into a few hundred thousand units, and each factor names a different budget line that has to be funded to move it.
terms.whyItMatters: Concept-test forecast questions supply the five percentages and expect the unit answer; walking the chain aloud is also how a plan defends why awareness money and distribution money are not substitutes for each other.

terms.definition: A schedule that alternates concentrated bursts with hiatus periods carrying no advertising at all — eight weeks on, four weeks dark — which buys higher in-season frequency than a flat continuous weight, at the cost of awareness decay during the dark weeks.
terms.whyItMatters: Seasonal-business roleplays turn on choosing this over pulsing or continuity, and the competitor is expected to name the trade the client is making rather than simply calling the plan seasonal.

terms.definition: Federal law requiring prior express written consent — signed, specific to marketing contact, and not made a condition of buying anything — before an autodialer or prerecorded message may call or text a mobile number, and requiring every seller to keep its own internal do-not-call list for five years. A checkbox buried in a purchase flow does not meet the standard.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-selling roleplay on texting a prospect list is graded on whether you ask how consent was captured; exam items contrast a consumer who bought something with one who signed a marketing permission.

terms.definition: Reached only when a table already satisfies first normal form, which removes repeating groups so each cell holds one value, and second normal form, which removes any non-key column depending on just part of a composite key, and then additionally removes transitive dependency — a non-key column determined by another non-key column rather than by the key.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam table showing a customer's ZIP code alongside the city that ZIP code determines is the classic normalization item, and the tested answer names which form that violation breaks.

terms.definition: The clock from a customer's message to the first substantive human reply, which stops on that reply even though nothing is fixed yet; resolution time runs on until the issue is actually closed. A 1-hour response with a 3-day resolution is a legitimate and common pair, and quoting one figure for both makes a team look twice as fast as it is.
terms.whyItMatters: Email and social-service roleplays set two separate targets, so a competitor who reports a single number has misread the case.

terms.definition: Applies stated go/no-go criteria to drop weak concepts before money is spent, and guards against two opposite errors -- a drop-error that kills a winner and a go-error that carries a loser into costly development; idea generation, by contrast, deliberately withholds all judgment to maximize the count.
terms.whyItMatters: A brainstorming roleplay is scored badly if you evaluate while generating; competitors must say which stage they are in and which error that stage is trying to avoid.

terms.definition: A one-sentence internal formula built from four required elements — the target segment, the frame of reference (the category the brand is to be compared against), the point of difference, and the reason to believe that substantiates it; drop the frame of reference and the claim has no competitive set to be better than, drop the reason to believe and it is an assertion. It is never customer-facing copy, which is the tagline's job.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges frequently ask a competitor to state the positioning out loud; delivering all four elements in one sentence is the difference between a scored answer and a slogan.

terms.definition: Auditing a small subset of items on a rotating schedule — high-value class A lines several times a year, class C lines once — so the business keeps operating, in contrast with a full physical count, which prices accuracy by shutting the facility for a wall-to-wall count once a year.
terms.whyItMatters: In a shrink-control roleplay the judge expects you to catch record errors continuously without closing the store, and to explain why the rotating audit finds problems months earlier than the annual shutdown.

terms.definition: (Price − marginal cost) ÷ price, running from 0 under perfect competition to near 1 for an unchallenged monopolist. A $50 price on $40 of marginal cost scores 0.20, and because the figure equals the reciprocal of demand elasticity, a firm facing elasticity of 5 can hold only a 20% markup over marginal cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing-power items ask how much a firm can charge above its own marginal cost, and the elasticity link converts a demand estimate into a markup ceiling.

terms.term: Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act
terms.definition: Federal statute obliging an employer of 100 or more employees to give 60 calendar days' written notice before a plant closing that ends 50 or more jobs at one site within any 30-day window, or a mass layoff of 500 workers — or of 50 to 499 when that reaches a third of the site's active workforce. Skipping notice is not a fine paid to the government: the remedy is back pay and benefits owed to each affected worker for every day of shortfall, capped at 60.
terms.whyItMatters: Worker-rights exam items use the 60-day count to kill distractors, and a professional-development roleplay where the judge plays an employee hearing closing rumors is scored on stating the notice entitlement and the back-pay remedy instead of offering reassurance.

terms.definition: Divide the population into naturally occurring groups such as stores, campuses or ZIP codes, randomly select a few of those groups, and survey everyone inside the selected ones; it costs far less per completed interview than stratified random sampling but carries a larger sampling error, because people inside one group resemble each other.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items on choosing a cost-effective field plan for a geographically spread customer base hinge on trading this design's cheapness against its wider error band.

terms.definition: Paid media spend divided by net sales, times 100, then benchmarked against the category norm — a 3% ratio in a category averaging 8% flags underinvestment. It counts media only, so it always reads lower than the marketing expense ratio for the same plan.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-review questions supply a company ratio and an industry average and ask whether spending is adequate; the comparison, not the raw number, is what earns the point.

terms.definition: A randomly selected slice of the target deliberately shown no advertising, so campaign lift is the exposed group's conversion rate minus the withheld group's — if exposed converts at 3.2% and the holdout at 2.6%, only 0.6 points were caused by the campaign and the rest would have happened anyway.
terms.whyItMatters: A client convinced a campaign drove every sale in its window is the setup for this method, and a competitor who can propose withholding a control group is answering a measurement question that platform-reported totals cannot.

terms.definition: Adding a product from a different category to the purchase — a case bought with a laptop — while upselling moves the customer up within the same line to a larger or higher-grade version of what they already chose. Suggestive selling covers both from the counter; the line that separates these two is category versus tier.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays scored on add-on sales ask you to name and demonstrate the technique, and calling a larger size a cross-sell is the error judges catch immediately.

terms.definition: Contacts passed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier divided by total contacts. A transfer moves a contact sideways to a peer queue; an escalation moves it up a level of authority — so an agent whose refund limit is $50 must escalate every $60 refund, and the rate is measuring the policy, not the customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about empowering frontline staff turn on this: raising an agent's approval limit is usually the cheapest way to cut it.

terms.definition: A design in which an employee reports to both a functional manager and a project or product manager at once, trading the single reporting line of a functional structure for cross-unit resource sharing, at the cost of dual-authority conflict and deliberate violation of unity of command.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about a staffer pulled between two bosses are scored on identifying the structure by name and proposing a priority-setting mechanism rather than a personality fix.

terms.definition: A finished business good that goes into another product and keeps its own identity there -- a car battery, a tire, a microchip; raw materials are processed until that identity is lost, and maintenance and repair supplies never enter the finished product at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Industrial product questions ask you to classify an input; the identity test decides it, and it also explains why component makers can advertise to the end consumer at all.

terms.definition: Values a brand as the licensing fee the owner avoids paying by owning it: forecast the revenue the brand will carry, multiply by an arm's-length royalty rate drawn from comparable licenses — commonly 2% to 6% of net sales — deduct tax, then discount the resulting stream to present value; unlike a cost-based valuation it ignores what was actually spent building the name, and unlike a market comparison it needs no sale of a similar brand.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking what the brand is worth on the balance sheet expects a named valuation method with its arithmetic, not the claim that a brand cannot be valued.

terms.definition: The network of people and activities moving a product from raw materials to the customer.
terms.whyItMatters: Supply-chain thinking underlies inventory, vendor, and cost decisions.

terms.definition: Extra output produced by one more worker, computed as the change in quantity divided by the change in workers. Going from 4 to 5 employees and from 40 to 46 units gives 6. It also sets marginal cost: at a $120 daily wage, that worker's units cost 120 ÷ 6 = $20 each, so cost per unit rises the moment the added output starts shrinking.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing and productivity items ask what one more scheduled worker actually adds and what that output costs, which is where diminishing returns become dollars.

terms.definition: Choose a random start inside the first interval, then take every kth record from the list, where k is the frame size divided by the sample size (a 12,000-name file sampled 400 times gives k = 30); the shortcut breaks when the list contains a repeating cycle that lines up with k, such as a roster ordered manager-then-staff.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a customer database and a target of 400 responses, an exam question expects the interval to be computed and the periodicity trap named.

terms.definition: The path a product takes from producer or provider to the final customer.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel choices affect convenience, cost, access, and customer experience.

terms.definition: Sets the average category buyer's annual purchase volume at 1.00 and states a brand's buyers against it, so 1.30 means the people who choose this brand buy 30% more of the category per year than the typical buyer; it is the third multiplier that converts a penetration figure and a repeat rate into a share estimate.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the factor students silently drop from a share forecast, turning a 12% answer into 10%, and it is the evidence behind a plan that argues for targeting heavy users instead of chasing more triers.

terms.definition: Google Ads' 1-to-10 diagnostic combining expected clickthrough rate, ad relevance and landing-page experience; it multiplies into the bid to set ad position, so an advertiser bidding $2.00 with a score of 8 outranks one bidding $3.00 with a score of 4 and pays less per click.
terms.whyItMatters: A search-advertising roleplay where the client wants to win position by raising the bid is the classic misread; the cheaper fix is tightening ad-to-keyword-to-page relevance, and the exam tests all three components by name.

terms.definition: Federal postal law lets anyone who receives goods they never ordered keep them as a free gift, with no duty to pay and no duty to ship them back, and a follow-up invoice creates no obligation. Only free samples plainly marked as such and merchandise sent by a charity asking for a donation fall outside it.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-and-ethical selling items describe a company mailing a product with a bill attached and ask what the recipient owes; a customer-complaint roleplay expects you to tell the caller the item is theirs.

terms.definition: Help-center or bot sessions that end without a human contact, divided by total sessions — 7,000 of 10,000 is 70%. A session only counts as deflected when no contact follows inside a set window, usually 24 hours; without that window an abandoned bot session where the customer gave up and phoned later is scored as a save.
terms.whyItMatters: The savings claim in a technology-in-CRM roleplay collapses without the follow-up window, and judges look for the competitor who states it.

terms.definition: Places a pre-release version with outside customers doing real work in their own conditions, capturing failures no internal lab reproduces; alpha testing comes first and is run in-house by employees, so a beta's whole value is the uncontrolled use an alpha deliberately excludes.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a limited launch is scored on why outside users are needed before full production, not merely on saying the product will be tested.

terms.definition: Cutting price below an appropriate measure of cost - courts generally use average variable cost - to drive rivals out, with a realistic prospect of recouping the losses later through higher prices. The Brooke Group standard requires both elements, which is what separates it from a loss leader, where a below-cost item exists only to pull traffic for other purchases.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-considerations questions turn on the recoupment element, so a candidate who simply says selling below cost is illegal is scored wrong.

terms.definition: Three decisions taken strictly in order — segment the market on one chosen base, target the segments worth serving against a stated attractiveness test, then position the offer against a named competitive set — where each step's output constrains the next; a positioning claim written before the segment is chosen has nobody in particular to be different for, which is why reordering the letters produces a plan that cannot be defended.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing-plan roleplays are graded on sequence as much as content; presenting a promotion idea before naming the segment invites the judge to ask who it is for.

terms.definition: Book inventory value minus counted physical value, divided by book value (or by net sales), expressed as a percentage — it isolates loss to theft, damage, spoilage and paperwork error, and never includes units legitimately sold.
terms.whyItMatters: Loss-prevention items give a recorded value and a counted value and ask for the percentage lost; the retail benchmark of roughly one to two percent of sales is what a judge compares your figure against.

terms.definition: Keep producing while the revenue the next unit brings in exceeds the cost it adds, and stop at the output where the two are equal. If the next unit adds $12 of revenue and $9 of cost, making it gains $3; past the crossing point each extra unit subtracts from profit even though total revenue is still rising.
terms.whyItMatters: Factors-affecting-profit items ask for the quantity a firm should produce from a marginal cost and marginal revenue schedule, not from total revenue.

terms.definition: Analysis of existing data from published reports, statistics, and studies.
terms.whyItMatters: It is cost-effective for understanding market context before original research.

terms.definition: Total marketing spend divided by net sales, times 100 — programs, salaries, agency fees and campaigns, not just media — so it answers what the plan costs to run. Marketing ROI asks the opposite question, what the same spend returned.
terms.whyItMatters: Control questions ask which metric shows a plan is over budget versus which shows it was unprofitable; naming the wrong one loses the item even when the arithmetic is right.

terms.definition: Requires verifiable parental consent before an operator collects personal information online from a child under 13, along with a clear privacy notice, a parent's right to review and delete what was collected, a ban on conditioning participation on handing over more data than needed, and reasonable retention limits. It binds sites directed at children and general-audience sites with actual knowledge of an under-13 user, and the FTC enforces it with civil penalties per violation.
terms.whyItMatters: A promotion roleplay for a children's product asks whether a sweepstakes entry form may collect email addresses at all.

terms.definition: Total spend divided by clicks received — $800 over 3,200 clicks is $0.25 — a pricing basis that charges only when someone acts, unlike cost per thousand, which charges for the impression whether or not anyone ever clicks it.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay asks which pricing model protects a small client's budget; the answer turns on whether the goal is awareness, where impressions are the product, or traffic, where only the click is worth paying for.

terms.definition: The reason a customer buys from this particular seller — service, location, reputation, staff knowledge or credit terms — as distinct from the product motive, which is the reason they want the item from anyone at all. A rep losing on patronage grounds cannot recover the sale by describing the product better.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying-behavior exam items sort a list of customer statements into the two motive types, and a roleplay customer who says a competitor is closer to home is testing whether you answer with service instead of features.

terms.definition: A grid that derives a case's priority from how many people or how much revenue is affected, set against how fast the situation degrades — high impact with high urgency becomes P1, high impact with low urgency P2, and so on across a 3x3 or 4x4 grid. Priority is computed from the two axes rather than argued by whoever complains loudest.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a backlog of angry customers in a roleplay, the competitor who sorts by this grid instead of by volume of complaint wins the judged point on fairness.

terms.definition: The contract section fixing measurable performance targets and the credit owed when they are missed: 99.9% monthly uptime allows roughly 43 minutes of outage in a 30-day month, and each tier missed below that refunds a stated percentage of the month's fee.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-services roleplays ask what the client is actually promised; converting a percentage into allowed minutes and naming the credit is what makes the promise enforceable.

terms.definition: The overall look and feel of a product or its packaging — the contour of a Coca-Cola bottle, a restaurant chain's interior scheme — protected under Lanham Act section 43(a) only when it is non-functional and has acquired secondary meaning in buyers' minds; product design trade dress can never be inherently distinctive, so unlike a coined word mark it always requires evidence that consumers link the look to a single source.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about a competitor copying a store's look are scored on naming this protection and its two conditions; calling it a trademark or a copyright is the common miss.

terms.definition: In Aristotle's Rhetoric, the persuasive material the speaker actually invents - ethos, the character the speaker projects; pathos, the emotion produced in the audience; and logos, the reasoning inside the message. It stands against inartistic proof, which the speaker only finds and presents: contracts, testimony, laws, prior statistics. The distinction matters because a weak case is repaired by inventing better proof of the first kind, never by restating the same evidence more loudly.
terms.whyItMatters: Presentation rubrics award points across all three, so a roleplay answer that is pure data with no credibility and no audience appeal caps out even when every number is right.

terms.definition: Coordination among suppliers, makers, and distributors to optimize flow and cut cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Collaboration reduces delays and strengthens competitive advantage.

terms.definition: Keep the doors open in the short run only while price covers average variable cost; at a lower price closing loses less, because fixed costs are owed either way. At $8 price with $7 variable and $4 fixed cost per unit, the firm loses $3 a unit but still operates, since shutting down would lose the full $4.
terms.whyItMatters: Operating-cost roleplays ask whether a location losing money should close now; the test is variable cost coverage, not whether the site is profitable.

terms.definition: Interviewers must fill preset counts per subgroup, say 120 women and 80 men, but pick the individual respondents themselves, so the subgroup proportions match the population while the selection itself stays nonprobability; stratified random sampling sets the very same proportions and then draws each person at random, which is what makes it projectable.
terms.whyItMatters: Mall-intercept and street-intercept scenarios in a research roleplay are this design, and the competitor is expected to name the limitation before quoting any percentage.

terms.definition: Scales a controlled market's result to a national number by dividing the test volume by that market's share of national category volume — 60,000 units in a market holding 2% of national volume projects to 3,000,000 units — then discounting for support levels, distribution or pricing that cannot be repeated nationwide.
terms.whyItMatters: Rollout questions give the test units plus the market's percentage of national volume and expect the projection; the discount step is what a judge presses on when a plan's national number looks suspiciously clean.

terms.definition: Opens divided by messages delivered — not messages sent — so 4,000 opens on 20,000 delivered is 20% while the same 4,000 against 25,000 sent looks like 16%. The count only fires when a tracking pixel loads, so image blocking and Apple's Mail Privacy Protection both distort it.
terms.whyItMatters: A direct-marketing roleplay reporting a suspiciously high figure after a privacy change is testing whether the competitor knows the metric is inferred from a pixel and will point to clicks as the reliable measure instead.

terms.definition: Short for best alternative to a negotiated agreement: the course of action you would actually take if these talks failed, which is what sets real bargaining power. It is not the price target and not the reservation price — the reservation price is the worst deal still worth accepting, derived from the alternative — and improving the outside option raises your power even if nothing at the table changes.
terms.whyItMatters: A supplier or salary negotiation roleplay is scored on the candidate knowing their walk-away option and estimating the other side's before conceding.

terms.definition: A selling arrangement in which silence counts as a yes — the seller announces the coming shipment and bills unless the buyer declines in time. It is lawful only if the buyer agreed to the terms up front, gets at least 10 days to reject each announced selection, and can cancel through a route as simple as the one used to enroll.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe a book or subscription club and ask what makes the automatic shipment legal; a subscription-selling roleplay is scored on disclosing the cancellation route before the customer signs.

terms.definition: A total outage or safety-affecting failure with no workaround, carrying the tightest published clock — commonly a 15-minute acknowledgement, hourly status updates and continuous work until restoration. Severity rates the technical damage while priority adds business context, so a Sev-1 affecting one tiny account can still be worked at P2.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-level roleplays hinge on the severity-versus-priority split, and quoting the acknowledgement clock is what makes the answer specific rather than reassuring.

terms.definition: Scores quality as perception minus expectation on paired 22-item scales across five dimensions -- reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy, responsiveness -- so a dimension scoring 0 means expectations were met exactly and every negative number is a measured shortfall to fix.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how you would measure service quality is scored on the subtraction: measuring satisfaction alone cannot tell an over-promise from an under-delivery.

terms.definition: Incremental gross profit from a campaign minus its marketing cost, divided by that marketing cost: $150,000 of incremental revenue at a 40% gross margin against $30,000 of spend is ($60,000 - $30,000) / $30,000, or 100%. It runs on margin rather than revenue, and only on the lift a holdout group shows the campaign actually caused, so a campaign whose sales would have happened anyway returns a negative figure no matter how large the revenue number looks.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks whether a promotion paid for itself, the graded answer is this ratio on margin with a baseline, not the raw sales the campaign period produced.

terms.definition: A card, bin or electronic signal that authorizes replenishment only after downstream consumption, making it a PULL system — the opposite of material requirements planning, which PUSHES output on a forecast whether or not the next station has consumed the last batch.
terms.whyItMatters: Production questions test the pull-versus-push distinction directly: the signal-driven system builds only what was used, so it is the answer when the scenario complains of piled-up work in process.

terms.definition: The yearly cost of borrowing stated as a percentage that folds in interest plus required fees, so two loans quoted at the same interest rate can carry different borrowing costs.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost-of-credit questions on the finance exam ask which loan is cheaper, and the answer is the one with the lower APR, not the lower nominal interest rate.

terms.definition: Selling price multiplied by the extra output the next worker adds — $15 a unit times 6 units is $90 a day. Hire while that figure is at or above the wage and stop when it drops below: at a $100 wage this worker is not worth adding, even though the worker before, adding 9 units and $135, clearly was.
terms.whyItMatters: Labor and productivity questions ask how many people a firm should employ, and the comparison of this figure to the wage is the tested rule.

terms.definition: The gap between a sample statistic and the true population value caused purely by which units happened to be drawn; it shrinks with the square root of sample size, so quadrupling the sample only halves it, and it is the single error a larger sample actually fixes, while nonsampling errors such as bad wording or a skewed list grow right along with scale.
terms.whyItMatters: Research-error questions ask which problems a bigger sample cures, and this is the only one on the list, so it separates the two error families in one stroke.

terms.definition: Averages the size of forecast misses ignoring their direction — the sum of |actual − forecast| ÷ the number of periods — which keeps the error in the product's own units instead of percentages, and roughly 1.25 times this figure approximates one standard deviation of forecast error for setting a buffer.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast-error items hand six periods of actuals and forecasts and expect this average computed; it is also the denominator of the tracking signal, so an error here quietly breaks the control check built on top of it.

terms.definition: Copies a publication actually distributes in an average issue, audited by the Alliance for Audited Media, as opposed to readership, which multiplies those copies by a pass-along factor of roughly 2 to 3 — so a 500,000-copy magazine can legitimately claim 1,200,000 readers.
terms.whyItMatters: Print-buying items give one vehicle's audited copies and a rival's claimed readers and ask which is the larger audience; the competitor has to convert both to the same basis before the cost-per-thousand comparison means anything.

terms.definition: Guidance requiring any material connection between an endorser and a seller — payment, free product, a job, a family tie — to be disclosed clearly and right next to the claim rather than buried in a profile or behind a More link, and requiring a testimonial showing unusual results to state what a typical buyer should expect.
terms.whyItMatters: A social-selling roleplay that has you brief an influencer is graded on where the disclosure sits; exam items ask whether a free product with no cash payment still has to be disclosed, and it does.

terms.definition: The mechanism that ties a state unemployment tax rate to an employer's own history of benefit charges — an employer that has laid off heavily may pay several times the rate of one that has not, on the same taxable wage base. Federal unemployment tax is 6.0% on the first $7,000 of each worker's wages, reduced by a 5.4% credit to a net 0.6%, or $42 per employee, when the state account is in good standing.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost questions about layoffs versus reduced hours turn on the rating consequence, which competitors usually miss by treating unemployment tax as a fixed cost.

terms.definition: The contractual penalty owed when a provider misses its service-level target — typically 10% of the monthly fee for the first missed tier, rising by band and capped at 100%. In most agreements it is the customer's sole remedy, and it must be claimed inside a stated window, often 30 days, or the right to it lapses entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-to-business account roleplay, the competitor who knows the credit must be requested rather than issued automatically recovers real money for the client.

terms.definition: Sells the finished product with its full marketing plan in a few representative cities while matched control cities keep the old plan, so the result read is the difference between the two areas rather than the test area's raw sales; the cost is secrecy, since rivals see the plan months early.
terms.whyItMatters: Launch roleplays ask how you would prove the plan works before national rollout; the matched control is the detail that turns a demo into a measurement.

terms.definition: Merchandise sold under the retailer's own name and sourced from a contract manufacturer, typically carrying a retail gross margin about 10 percentage points above the comparable national brand — roughly 35% against 25% — while retailing 15% to 30% cheaper, because the retailer carries no national advertising cost; the national brand by contrast is owned, advertised and priced by the manufacturer, who keeps that margin.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays about shelf space are settled with this margin arithmetic, and a competitor who argues only that the store brand is cheaper has missed why the retailer prefers it.

terms.definition: An organization-wide commitment to continuous improvement and quality.
terms.whyItMatters: A quality culture lowers defects and lifts loyalty over time.

terms.definition: The smallest output at which long-run average cost stops falling and flattens out. If unit cost drops from $9 to $6 between 10,000 and 50,000 units and then holds at $6, the threshold is 50,000 — a rival producing 20,000 pays $7 or $8 and cannot match a $6.50 price, which is how the number becomes an entry barrier.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition items ask why a small entrant cannot match an incumbent's price, and the expected answer is the output threshold, not brand loyalty.

terms.definition: An organized, computer-managed collection of related data that can be stored and retrieved systematically.
terms.whyItMatters: Businesses run everything from inventory to customer records on databases.

terms.definition: Methods that explore motivations and attitudes through open-ended responses.
terms.whyItMatters: Qualitative insight reveals why customers decide, sharpening messaging.

terms.definition: (actual minus planned) / planned x 100, carried on every line of the marketing plan: $92,000 delivered against a $100,000 forecast is -8%. The sign alone does not say good or bad — negative on revenue is unfavorable, negative on expense is favorable.
terms.whyItMatters: Mid-year review items give planned and actual columns and ask which lines need action; competitors who read every negative as a problem flag the underspent line that is actually helping.

terms.definition: An email permanently rejected because the address does not exist or the domain is dead, as opposed to a soft bounce, which is a temporary failure such as a full mailbox or a server outage and gets retried; mailbox providers begin filtering a sender whose permanent-failure rate passes roughly 2%.
terms.whyItMatters: A client whose newsletter suddenly lands in spam usually has an unpurged list, and a direct-marketing roleplay expects the competitor to distinguish the two failure types before recommending list hygiene.

terms.definition: Months a newly hired rep needs before carrying full quota, credited in steps — commonly no quota in the first quarter, half in the second and full in the third. A rep hired in March therefore contributes roughly a quarter of an annual number that year, which is why headcount added late almost never rescues a current-year gap.
terms.whyItMatters: Sales-management items ask what revenue a mid-year hire adds this year, and the credit schedule is the whole answer; a roleplay on onboarding new sellers expects you to name the stepped quota rather than promise full production on day one.

terms.definition: The finding that a customer whose problem is fixed exceptionally well can finish more loyal than one who never had a problem — but it holds only for a first, low-severity failure resolved fast by someone empowered to fix it on the spot. On a repeat failure the effect reverses and satisfaction lands below the never-failed baseline, so engineering failures is never the strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Complaint roleplays reward naming the condition; a competitor who claims the paradox always applies is marked down for it.

terms.definition: An employer rule capping what any manager may tell a reference checker — dates of employment, job title, and sometimes final pay — adopted because a former employer's comment on performance holds its qualified privilege only while made in good faith and loses it, opening a defamation claim, once malice or reckless falsehood is shown. It is not a universal shield: a handful of states run service-letter statutes, Missouri's being the model, that compel a letter stating the cause of separation within 45 days of a certified-mail request from anyone who worked at least 90 days.
terms.whyItMatters: Professional-development roleplays hand the competitor a manager who wants to warn another firm about a fired employee, and the graded answer is the disclosure limit plus the legal reason for it; job-search exam items use the same rule to explain why a former supervisor will confirm only dates.

terms.definition: Locates a failure in one of five gaps -- not knowing what customers expect, setting wrong standards, delivery that misses those standards, promotion promising what operations cannot deliver, and the customer gap between expectation and perception, which is produced by the first four.
terms.whyItMatters: Guest-recovery roleplays are scored on diagnosing which gap caused the complaint, since an over-promising ad and an untrained server call for opposite fixes.

terms.definition: The sum of the discounted lifetime values of a firm's current and future customers — the asset value of the customer base itself — which can rise while brand equity falls, as when a firm buys volume with deep discounts and wins customers who think less of the name each year; brand equity is the value held in what buyers believe about the mark, customer equity the value held in the relationships and their future cash.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked whether a discount-driven growth plan is healthy, the judged answer separates the two equities and says which one the plan is spending down.

terms.definition: A physical or software constraint that makes the wrong action impossible or immediately obvious — a plug that only fits one way, a field that refuses an invalid date — so defects are PREVENTED at the source, unlike statistical process control, which detects defects after they have already been produced.
terms.whyItMatters: Quality-method questions distinguish prevention from detection, and the mistake-proofing device is the accepted example of prevention when a scenario describes a repeated human error.

terms.definition: Gap between what buyers would have paid and what they did pay, measured as the area under the demand curve and above the market price. With demand starting at $50, a $20 price and 300 units sold, it equals ½ × 300 × ($50 − $20) = $4,500 — and a price rise to $30 cuts it, which is the value a seller captures when it segments buyers.
terms.whyItMatters: Price-function questions ask what buyers lose when a price rises or a shortage appears; the triangle turns that into a dollar figure.

terms.definition: The plus-or-minus band reported around a survey percentage, calculated as a z value times the square root of p(1 - p)/n, which works out to roughly plus or minus 3.1 points on a sample of 1,000 at 95% confidence; it describes precision only, so it says nothing whatever about bias in who chose to respond.
terms.whyItMatters: Interpreting a research finding for a client, a competitor who reports 46% without the band, or who treats a 2-point lead inside the band as a real lead, loses the point.

terms.definition: Barney's resource test asking whether a resource is Valuable, Rare, costly to Imitate, and whether the Organization is arranged to exploit it; a resource that is valuable and rare but cheap to copy yields only temporary advantage, while all four yield sustained advantage.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions describe a resource a rival duplicated within a year and expect you to say which VRIO letter it failed and what that means for advantage.

terms.definition: Divides the running cumulative forecast error by the mean absolute deviation to test whether misses are random noise or one-sided drift; a value wandering past ±4 says the model is systematically off and must be re-fit rather than nudged, while a value oscillating around zero says the error is noise and the model should be left alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast-control questions supply a cumulative error and a MAD and want both the ratio and the keep-or-refit call against the limit, not a general remark that the forecast looks wrong.

terms.definition: A medium's published open prices per unit of time or space, quoted before any negotiation; national buyers routinely settle 30% to 50% under them, so a media plan costed at these published figures overstates what the buy will actually cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a small client is handed a station's published prices tests whether the competitor knows the quoted number is an opening position, and a plan built on it will look unaffordable when it is not.

terms.definition: The sales-tax duty a seller picks up in a state where it owns no building and employs no one, triggered purely by volume — commonly $100,000 of sales or 200 separate transactions into that state in the current or prior year. Cross the threshold and the seller must register, collect and remit there; a purely online business is not exempt.
terms.whyItMatters: E-commerce selling items give a state-by-state sales table and ask where tax must now be collected; an expansion roleplay expects you to raise registration before recommending a push into a new state.

terms.definition: The measured gap between complaints received and customers actually dissatisfied — the classic TARP studies put the share of unhappy customers who bother to complain at roughly 4 in 100, so one voiced complaint stands in for about two dozen silent defectors. A falling complaint count can therefore signal abandonment rather than improvement.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay that celebrates fewer complaints needs this correction, and it is the argument that funds proactive outreach.

terms.definition: Something buyers do not think to look for and may not know exists, so it has to be sold to them rather than bought -- burial plots, life insurance, a brand-new category's first entrant; a specialty good is the opposite pole, actively hunted by name with special effort.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling roleplays for insurance or services are scored on recognizing that no one walks in asking, which forces prospecting and personal selling rather than displays.

terms.definition: An intermediary that helps buy or sell on a producer's behalf without taking title to goods.
terms.whyItMatters: Agents lower channel cost by handling transactions without holding inventory.

terms.definition: The share and cost lead a pioneer can lock in through buyer switching costs, scarce shelf space or spectrum, and a learning-curve cost position — but Golder and Tellis found market pioneers failed roughly 47% of the time and held about 10% share on average, while the fast follower entering after the category's standard settles skips the cost of educating the market and buys the pioneer's proof of demand for free.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about racing a competitor to launch expect both sides argued with evidence; asserting that being first always wins is the answer the data contradicts.

terms.definition: A Pareto split of stock by annual dollar usage: roughly the top 20 percent of items carrying about 80 percent of the value are class A and get tight control and frequent counts, class B moderate control, class C the low-value bulk that is managed loosely with large buffers.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how a warehouse manager should spend limited counting and control effort, the accepted answer is to classify by dollar usage and concentrate on class A rather than treat every item alike.

terms.definition: Area between the equal-shares diagonal and the actual income curve, divided by the whole triangle under that diagonal, giving 0 for identical incomes and 1 for one household holding everything. A move from 0.38 to 0.45 means income concentrated, and since it is a ratio it says nothing about whether anyone got richer.
terms.whyItMatters: Economic-development items compare two markets' income spread to pick a target segment, and the score is the measure they hand you.

terms.definition: The range a statistic is expected to occupy, such as 42% plus or minus 3 points meaning 39% to 45%, while the confidence level is the separate 95% or 99% figure describing how often intervals built this way capture the true value; raising the level widens the range at the same sample size, so more certainty always costs precision.
terms.whyItMatters: Presenting findings to a manager who wants a single number, the tested skill is stating the range and the level as two different things rather than collapsing them.

terms.definition: Scores every step of a forecasting process by the accuracy points it adds over the naive baseline — baseline MAPE 20%, statistical model 17%, sales-team override 19% — so the model step is worth +3 points and the override is worth −2 and should be removed from the process rather than coached.
terms.whyItMatters: Process-improvement items ask which forecasting step to cut, and the negative-value step is the answer; it is also the numeric way a plan review argues that field overrides are hurting the number instead of helping it.

terms.definition: Restricts a category to a few preset price points - say $29, $59 and $99 - and buys merchandise to fit them rather than pricing each item off its own cost. Psychological tactics change the digits shown at a single price point, whereas this decides how many price points the assortment offers at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Apparel-buying roleplays ask how a store can carry forty styles without paralyzing shoppers, and the answer is the number of price points rather than the number of items.

terms.definition: The 2003 federal statute governing commercial email: every message needs truthful headers and subject line, a valid physical postal address, and an opt-out mechanism honored within 10 business days, with civil penalties assessed per individual message sent rather than per campaign.
terms.whyItMatters: An email-promotion roleplay where a client wants to keep mailing customers who unsubscribed is a compliance question with a specific deadline attached, and the per-message penalty structure is what makes a single bad send expensive.

terms.definition: One deal's single commission pool divided between the rep who sourced it and the rep who closed it — 50/50, 30/70 or whatever the plan states — and the shares must total 100 percent. It changes who gets paid, never how much the company pays out, which is exactly the point students miss when they assume both reps earn a full commission.
terms.whyItMatters: Compensation items give a deal value, a commission rate and two named reps and check whether you double the payout; a team-selling roleplay expects you to settle credit before the sale, not after.

terms.definition: Lapsed customers who return after a targeted campaign, divided by lapsed customers contacted — 120 of 2,000 is 6%. It usually beats new acquisition on cost because the contact data and purchase history are already owned, but only when the offer answers the stated reason for leaving rather than simply discounting the same product.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay asks which list gets the budget, and this rate weighed against customer acquisition cost is the comparison judges expect.
