terms.definition: The band between desired service, what the customer hopes for, and adequate service, the least they will accept: performance inside the band passes unnoticed, above it delights, below it triggers complaint or defection, and the band narrows sharply in urgent or first-time-fix situations.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about exceeding guest expectations are scored on knowing that ordinary delivery earns nothing; the band explains why effort spent in the middle is invisible.

terms.definition: A brand's share of category advertising spend minus its share of category sales — 12% of spend against 8% of sales gives +4 points. Binet and Field's analysis of IPA effectiveness cases found roughly every 10 points of positive excess buys about half a point of annual market-share growth, so a brand that holds its budget flat while rivals raise theirs loses share on an unchanged budget because the metric is relative, not absolute.
terms.whyItMatters: Budget roleplays that propose holding advertising spend steady are answered with this relative measure, which shows why a flat budget is a cut in competitive terms.

terms.definition: A court's power over the defendant rather than over the dispute, established by presence, domicile, consent, or the minimum-contacts standard from International Shoe, under which the defendant purposefully availed itself of the forum state and the claim arises from those contacts. Subject-matter jurisdiction is the separate question of whether the court may hear that kind of case at all — federal diversity jurisdiction, for example, demands complete diversity plus more than $75,000 in controversy.
terms.whyItMatters: Judicial-system exam items ask where an online seller can be dragged into court after shipping into another state.

terms.definition: A doctrine holding that one bottleneck sets the output of the whole system, worked through five focusing steps — identify the constraint, exploit it, subordinate everything else to it, elevate it with added capacity, then repeat because the constraint has moved — so improvement anywhere else adds inventory, not throughput.
terms.whyItMatters: When a production roleplay describes one slow station, the judge wants the constraint named and the rest of the line paced to it, not a blanket speed-up of every station.

terms.definition: Allocate a budget so the last dollar spent on each good returns the same added satisfaction: MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py. If one item returns 20 utils per dollar and another 10, shifting spending toward the first raises total satisfaction until the two ratios meet — the rule that produces the downward-sloping demand curve.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying-behavior roleplays ask why a shopper walked away from the better product; the per-dollar comparison, not the raw benefit, explains the switch.

terms.definition: Methods that measure numeric data through surveys and statistical analysis.
terms.whyItMatters: Quantitative findings give statistical proof to justify marketing decisions.

terms.definition: The geographic zone a location actually draws customers from, mapped as rings: the primary ring supplies roughly 60-75% of customers, the secondary another 15-25%, and the fringe the scattered remainder. It sets the population a site's forecast is allowed to count.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-selection and retail-expansion cases give customer ZIP-code counts and ask how far the draw reaches; forecasting against the whole metropolitan population instead of the primary ring inflates every downstream number.

terms.definition: Replacement time or space a medium owes when a commitment ran in the wrong position, ran late, or fell short of guaranteed delivery — a station that guarantees 150 gross rating points and delivers 120 owes those 30 points back as inventory, not as a cash refund.
terms.whyItMatters: An under-delivery roleplay tests whether the competitor asks for the right remedy; demanding money back where the contract promises replacement inventory usually forfeits the claim entirely.

terms.definition: One of the four rules Paul Grice argued every speaker in a cooperative exchange is assumed to be following: quantity (say as much as is needed and no more), quality (say only what you believe true and can support), relation (stay relevant) and manner (be brief, orderly and unambiguous). Meaning rides on a broken rule as much as a kept one - an unusually short answer to 'how did the interview go' communicates trouble precisely because it violates quantity.
terms.whyItMatters: Items about reading between the lines of a customer's reply, or about why an over-detailed email starts to sound evasive, are testing these four rules by name.

terms.definition: A municipal rule making uninvited door-to-door solicitation of a home unlawful, so a canvasser needs a local permit or an invitation from the occupant before knocking. Courts have upheld these ordinances, and violating one is an offense in that town even when the product, the price and the sales pitch are all perfectly legitimate.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-and-ethical selling items place a canvassing crew in a town with such an ordinance and ask what must happen first; a field-selling roleplay expects permits checked before a neighborhood route is planned.

terms.definition: A refund, credit or replacement granted where the company owes nothing contractually — outside warranty, past the return window, or where the customer caused the damage. It is expensed as a service or marketing cost rather than charged against the warranty reserve, which is why finance tracks it separately and caps each agent's authority in dollars.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the customer's claim is genuinely out of policy tests whether the competitor can grant an exception and state what it costs the company.

terms.definition: A tangible item expected to survive repeated use, the standard statistical cutoff being an expected life of three years or more, which is why appliances and vehicles qualify; nondurables are consumed in one or a few uses and are bought on habit rather than deliberation.
terms.whyItMatters: Warranty, financing, and personal-selling effort all follow this split, so an exam item on why one product gets a service plan and another does not is answered with the three-year line.

terms.definition: Ehrenberg's empirical finding that a brand with a smaller customer base is punished twice over — fewer people buy it at all, and those who do buy it less often — so measured loyalty is almost entirely a consequence of penetration rather than an independent lever; the practical consequence is that a small brand's plan to grow purely by deepening loyalty among existing buyers contradicts the pattern found in essentially every category studied.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a retention-only growth plan for a small brand is a trap; naming this regularity and redirecting toward penetration is the scored move.

terms.definition: Scheduling deliveries to arrive as production consumes them so carrying cost and warehouse space approach zero; the explicit trade against safety-stock buffering is that it removes the cushion that absorbs a late supplier, so one disrupted shipment stops the line.
terms.whyItMatters: A supply-disruption roleplay wants both halves — the carrying-cost saving and the exposure it creates — because recommending it without naming the supplier-reliability requirement is what costs the point.

terms.definition: Over-weighting a person's character and under-weighting their circumstances when explaining someone else's behavior — the late colleague is careless rather than stuck behind an accident. Its mirror image applied to oneself is the self-serving bias, and together the pair make an appraisal reward good luck and punish bad context.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item asking why a supervisor rates a rep poorly after a territory loses its largest account expects this bias by name, and roleplays on fair evaluation reward asking about conditions before judging the person.

terms.definition: Tangible products in limited supply that must be produced and purchased.
terms.whyItMatters: Distinguishing goods from services underlies every business model.

terms.definition: Measurement that has equal intervals and a true zero, as with dollars spent, units purchased or minutes in store, so ratios carry meaning and one shopper can correctly be said to spend twice what another does; an interval scale such as a 1-to-7 rating has equal spacing but an arbitrary zero, so averaging is legitimate while twice as satisfied is not.
terms.whyItMatters: Descriptive-statistics items test which arithmetic a given measure permits, and the classic trap is multiplying or dividing rating-scale scores as though they behaved like dollars.

terms.definition: Divides the standard deviation of period demand by its mean to grade how forecastable a series is: under about 0.25 a single point forecast is dependable, and above roughly 0.50 the item is erratic enough that the plan must carry a range and a buffer instead of one number.
terms.whyItMatters: Planning questions ask which item deserves a statistical forecast and which needs judgment plus safety stock; the ratio decides it, and the threshold is the part of the item being tested.

terms.definition: The FTC doctrine that an advertiser must already hold the evidence for an objective claim before that claim runs, and that health or performance claims require competent and reliable scientific evidence — the line separating a provable assertion from puffery, which makes no measurable claim and needs no proof.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay client who wants to advertise that a product works twice as fast is asking a legal question, and the competitor is scored on requiring the proof up front rather than promising to find it if challenged.

terms.definition: Plan language reversing commission already paid when the customer cancels or fails to pay inside a stated chargeback window — often 90 days for non-payment or the first 12 months of a subscription. Once that window closes the money is the rep's to keep, so the length of the window, not the cancellation itself, decides whether the company recovers anything.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics-and-compensation items ask what happens when a rep sells to a customer who churns in month two, and the answer depends on the window; a roleplay on writing a commission plan is graded on naming one.

terms.definition: Spreading investments across different assets to reduce overall risk.
terms.whyItMatters: Diversification is the standard answer to lowering investment risk in finance events.

terms.definition: The share of customers who buy again inside a defined window, counted per purchase occasion — 30 of 100 first-time buyers ordering again within 90 days is 30%. Retention rate counts customers still active at period end whether or not they bought anything, so a subscription can post 95% retention alongside a repurchase rate of zero.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty cases mix the two constantly, and naming the difference in the denominator is the discriminating answer a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: The severest federal recall classification, used when a defect carries a reasonable probability of serious injury or death; Class II covers defects whose harm is temporary or medically reversible and where serious harm is remote, and Class III covers violations unlikely to cause any harm.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-protection questions give a defect scenario and ask how urgently the firm must act; the class decides the notification reach and the speed regulators expect.

terms.definition: A comprehensive, systematic, independent and periodic examination of a firm's whole marketing environment, objectives, strategies and activities — all four adjectives are required, so a review of one campaign conducted by the team that ran it qualifies as none of them; its deliverable is a ranked list of corrective actions, not a score or a performance rating.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks how you would diagnose a marketing department that is missing its targets, the independence and scope conditions are what distinguish an audit from an internal post-mortem.

terms.definition: Available production time in a shift divided by customer units demanded in that shift — the pace demand dictates, which is set outside the factory, unlike cycle time, the pace the line actually achieves; a cycle time above it means the plant cannot keep up with orders.
terms.whyItMatters: Line-balancing items give shift minutes and a daily order quantity and ask how often a unit must come off the line; confusing the demand-set pace with the observed one flips the answer.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by the required reserve ratio, and caps how far one new deposit can expand the money supply: at a 10% reserve ratio the multiplier is 10, so $1,000 of fresh reserves can support up to $10,000 of deposits. Cash held outside banks and excess reserves both shrink the real-world figure below the formula.
terms.whyItMatters: Macro items that hand you a reserve ratio and a deposit want this reciprocal computed, and the deposit-expansion number is graded, not the explanation of lending.

terms.definition: A selection interview in which every candidate receives the same predetermined questions in the same order and answers are scored against written anchors, rather than the interviewer following the conversation wherever it goes. Research places its predictive validity near .51 against roughly .38 for the unstructured version, and the fixed script is also what makes the process defensible when a rejected applicant alleges disparate treatment.
terms.whyItMatters: A hiring roleplay asking how to make interviews fairer is answered by fixing the question set and the scoring key, not by adding a second interviewer.

terms.definition: Asymmetry in a distribution that drags the mean away from the middle, so a handful of $900 orders inside a file of $30 orders pulls the mean above the median and the median becomes the honest typical figure; income, home price and basket-size data are routinely reported this way, while the mean suits data that is roughly symmetric.
terms.whyItMatters: Presenting an average order value that no actual customer resembles is the classic descriptive-statistics error a judge probes, and the answer is which measure of center fits the shape.

terms.definition: Personal income for an area minus personal tax payments — the disposable dollars residents can actually spend, not gross earnings. It is the income term inside a buying power index, which weights it against the area's population and retail sales.
terms.whyItMatters: Territory and market-selection items give gross income for two cities and expect the after-tax spendable figure to drive the ranking, because a high-tax market supports less spending than its wage level suggests.

terms.definition: Coverage, mentions and shares a brand receives without buying placement — as against paid media, which is bought inventory the brand controls outright, and owned media, which is the brand's own site, list and channels. Only the paid third can be guaranteed to appear on a chosen date.
terms.whyItMatters: A launch-planning roleplay that leans on press pickup for a fixed launch day is the trap this term defends against, and public-relations items on the exam expect the three-way split to be named, not just the unpaid half.

terms.definition: Under the UCC a seller sheds merchantability only with conspicuous language that actually uses the word merchantability, or with an as-is / with-all-faults notice, and sheds fitness for a particular purpose only in writing. An express promise once made cannot be disclaimed at all — fine print cannot cancel what the salesperson said out loud.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a spoken performance promise with an as-is sticker and ask which survives; a product-selling roleplay is scored on not making a claim the contract cannot later walk back.

terms.definition: A published schedule matching the size of the failure to the size of the fix — apology plus correction for a minor first delay, a partial credit of roughly 10% to 25% of the transaction for a repeat, and a full refund plus a retention offer where the failure cost the customer money. It keeps compensation consistent and stops the loudest complainer being paid the most.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges in complaint roleplays reward a proportionate remedy; naming the rung and its value beats offering a blanket refund every time.

terms.definition: The four guarantees a relational transaction makes — atomicity, meaning all steps commit or none do; consistency, meaning no declared rule is left broken; isolation, meaning concurrent transactions cannot read each other's partial work; and durability, meaning a committed write survives a crash — and precisely the set that BASE-style distributed stores relax in exchange for availability.
terms.whyItMatters: A banking-transfer scenario asks what keeps a debit from posting when the matching credit fails, and the graded answer names atomicity within this set rather than saying the system is careful.

terms.definition: The Consumer Product Safety Act duty to notify the Commission within 24 hours of obtaining information that a product contains a defect creating a substantial hazard, fails a mandatory standard, or poses an unreasonable risk -- and the duty applies even when the firm still disputes the defect.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics and consumer-protection roleplays test whether you report before finishing your own investigation; waiting for certainty is the answer that loses the indicator and, in practice, draws the fine.

terms.definition: Rogers' model dividing adopters over time into five fixed bands measured in standard deviations from the mean adoption date — innovators 2.5%, early adopters 13.5%, early majority 34%, late majority 34% and laggards 16% — so the opinion-leading early adopters are a narrow 13.5% band that must be won before the 34% early majority will move, and a launch plan aimed at the mass market from day one is aimed at people who are not yet buying.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product roleplays ask who to target first; naming the band and its percentage is what turns 'we'll target trendsetters' into a defensible answer.

terms.definition: Availability multiplied by performance multiplied by quality, each a percentage — so a machine running 90 percent uptime at 90 percent of rated speed with 90 percent good output scores about 73 percent, which is why the product exposes losses the three separate rates hide.
terms.whyItMatters: Equipment and maintenance questions ask why a line reported as 'ninety percent up' still misses its quota; multiplying the three loss categories is the accepted way to show it.

terms.definition: How many times the average dollar is spent on final goods and services in a year, computed as nominal GDP divided by the money supply. It is the V in the equation of exchange MV = PQ, so when V is stable, growth in the money supply passes straight through into higher prices.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation items that ask why a large increase in the money supply did not produce proportional price increases are asking the competitor to reason about a fall in this ratio.

terms.definition: Selecting a representative subset of a population to study instead of everyone.
terms.whyItMatters: Sound sampling cuts cost and time while keeping conclusions valid.

terms.definition: The line of authority defining who reports to whom in an organization.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing when and how to escalate is a frequent judgment point in roleplays.

terms.definition: Splits a revenue miss into three computed pieces that must add back to the total gap: price variance = (actual price − planned price) × actual units; volume variance = (actual units − planned units) × planned price; mix variance = the shift in each product's share of total units valued at planned prices.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-review items give planned and actual price, units and product split and expect all three figures; answering that sales came in soft without the decomposition is exactly what the rubric withholds credit for.

terms.definition: The share of a rebate offer's buyers who qualify but never file the paperwork, which is why a $50 mail-in rebate with 40% of buyers never claiming actually costs the manufacturer $30 per unit sold — the gap between a promotion's face value and its real cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A pricing-and-promotion roleplay comparing an instant discount against a mail-in offer of the same face value turns on this: the two look identical to the customer and cost the manufacturer very different amounts.

terms.definition: A tiered approval ladder capping how deep each level may cut price before escalating — a rep to 10 percent, a sales manager to 20, a vice president to 30, and anything past that to finance. Margin is protected by who is allowed to sign, not by how well an individual rep negotiates, so a buyer stalling for more has to be moved up the ladder.
terms.whyItMatters: A price-negotiation roleplay where the buyer demands 25 percent off is scored on whether you know you must escalate instead of conceding; pricing items test the ladder as a control on gross margin.

terms.definition: The support, delivery, returns and account-management cost attributable to one customer or segment, subtracted after cost of goods before any margin judgement — a segment buying $50,000 at 30% gross margin but generating $12,000 of returns and service calls earns $3,000, not $15,000. Revenue rank and profit rank routinely disagree because of it.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains why the largest account in a case can be the unprofitable one, and any roleplay recommending a service fee or a channel change for that account has to show this subtraction.

terms.definition: Nothing can be inspected, weighed, or returned before purchase, so buyers judge search qualities beforehand, experience qualities only during delivery, and credence qualities -- a surgeon's technique, a tax opinion -- never at all; a good lets buyers verify most attributes before paying.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay contrasting service marketing with product marketing is scored on the tangible cues you add -- uniforms, facilities, guarantees -- to stand in for inspection.

terms.definition: Drucker's cascade in which manager and employee jointly set specific, measurable, time-bound goals aligned to company objectives and review results against those goals at period end, so appraisal rests on agreed output rather than on the supervisor's trait ratings.
terms.whyItMatters: Management roleplays that ask how to raise an underperforming team's accountability are scored on the joint goal-setting step, which is exactly what separates this from a top-down quota.

terms.definition: Any contact at which a buyer forms a judgment about a brand with no marketing message present to help — Procter & Gamble named the 3 to 7 seconds facing the shelf the first such moment and the first use of the product the second; the practical rule is that advertising spend cannot repair a touchpoint at which the customer has already decided against the brand.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about check-in or complaint handling are scored on identifying the exact contact that decides the guest's opinion and fixing that, not on adding promotion.

terms.definition: Continuous small improvements generated by the workers doing the job, accumulating gradually at near-zero capital cost — deliberately opposed to kaikaku or reengineering, which is a rare, top-down, capital-heavy redesign of the whole process.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks how to streamline work without a budget, the incremental frontline approach is the fitting recommendation, and the judge listens for why you did not propose a full redesign.

terms.definition: The inputs — land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship — used to produce goods and services.
terms.whyItMatters: Managing limited resources is central to operations and strategy.

terms.definition: The square root of the average squared distance of the observations from their mean, expressed in the same units as the data, and in a roughly normal distribution about 68% of cases fall within one of them and 95% within two; it converts a bare average satisfaction of 4.1 into a statement about how consistent the experience actually is.
terms.whyItMatters: Two locations with identical mean scores but different spread call for different management action, and interpreting research findings for a client rests on saying so.

terms.definition: Isolates the profit effect of selling a different blend than planned: for each item, (its actual share of total units − its planned share) × total actual units × that item's planned contribution per unit, summed across the line — so a firm can hit its unit target exactly and still miss profit by shifting volume onto the thinner-margin product.
terms.whyItMatters: Shortfall questions where total units met plan are solved with this term alone, and it is the numeric case for paying sales incentives on contribution rather than on units sold.

terms.definition: A distribution path where a producer sells straight to customers with no intermediaries.
terms.whyItMatters: Direct channels maximize control and margin but demand more sales and logistics effort.

terms.definition: Paid placement built to match the form and feel of the surrounding editorial content, which the FTC requires be labeled Ad, Sponsored or Paid before the reader clicks — precisely because matching the publisher's format is what stops a reader from telling it apart from unpaid editorial.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay proposing an article that reads like the site's own reporting is scored on whether the competitor puts the disclosure ahead of the click, and exam items contrast it with publicity, which is unpaid and carries no label duty.

terms.definition: An inquiry the sales team has formally accepted after confirming a named need, a budget owner and a decision timeline, where a marketing-qualified lead has cleared only a behavior score such as downloads or page visits. Handoff agreements usually give sales a fixed window, often 24 hours, to accept it or send it back with a stated reason.
terms.whyItMatters: Funnel items ask at which stage marketing's responsibility ends and sales' begins; a roleplay on fixing a marketing-sales dispute is scored on defining the acceptance criteria and the return window.

terms.definition: Customers who bring in at least one new paying customer, divided by total customers — 400 of 8,000 is 5%, and it can never exceed 100% because it counts referrers. The viral coefficient counts new customers produced per existing customer instead, so it can exceed 1; quoting one where the other belongs makes a growth forecast impossible.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth roleplays ask for a measurable target, and the wrong one of the two makes the projection arithmetically unachievable.

terms.definition: A label a written warranty may carry only if it repairs defects free within a reasonable time, puts no duty on the buyer beyond giving notice, does not limit the duration of implied warranties, and offers a refund or replacement after a reasonable number of failed repairs; missing any one forces the 'limited' label.
terms.whyItMatters: Warranty roleplays ask what a store may print on the tag; a written warranty that charges a handling fee cannot be called full, and knowing which of the four conditions broke is the scoring point.

terms.definition: Moore's gap between the 13.5% early-adopter band, which buys on the promise of a breakthrough and tolerates an incomplete product, and the 34% early majority, which buys only on references from people already like themselves; products stall in it because the two groups will not act as references for each other, and the standard bridge is dominating one narrow beachhead segment until its references become credible to the next group.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay shows strong early sales that suddenly flatten, naming this gap and the beachhead fix is the diagnosis a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: A supplier's agreement with its dealers fixing the minimum price they may resell at. The Leegin decision moved minimum RPM from per se illegal to a rule-of-reason analysis under federal law, though several states still bar it outright; a minimum advertised price policy differs because it restricts only the advertised figure and leaves the checkout price free.
terms.whyItMatters: Manufacturer-channel roleplays ask whether a brand may stop a discounter from undercutting its dealers, and the answer depends on this distinction.

terms.definition: Software that explodes a master production schedule through the bill of materials and nets it against on-hand stock to time component orders; it plans materials only, while enterprise resource planning extends the same database to finance, human resources and sales as one system.
terms.whyItMatters: Technology-in-operations items test whether you can scope the two acronyms apart — the narrow materials planner versus the company-wide platform — which is the discrimination most competitors get backwards.

terms.definition: The relationship stating that the real interest rate equals the nominal rate minus expected inflation, so a savings account paying 7% during 5% inflation earns only about 2% in purchasing power — and a 3% account during 4% inflation loses money in real terms even though the balance grows.
terms.whyItMatters: A personal-finance or economics item that gives a stated rate and an inflation rate is asking for the real return; answering with the posted nominal rate is the standard miss.

terms.definition: A single number running from -1 through 0 to +1 that measures how tightly two variables move together, with 0 meaning no linear relationship; squaring it gives the share of variation explained, so a value of 0.6 accounts for only 36% of the movement, and even a value near 1 establishes association and never that one variable caused the other.
terms.whyItMatters: Handed an output showing ad spend and sales at 0.72, the tested response reports the strength, converts it to explained variation, and refuses the causal claim.

terms.definition: The average signed error across periods — actual minus forecast with the plus and minus signs kept — so persistent over-forecasting shows up as a running negative. It measures direction, where MAPE measures size, and a plan can post a respectable MAPE while drifting the same way every single month.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast-review items give a run of months that miss high every time and ask what is wrong with the method; the answer is a systematic error in the assumptions, not random noise.

terms.definition: Loyalty points, gift-card balances and promotional credits that were issued but are never redeemed and eventually release to revenue; a program booking 15% and then seeing only 5% has understated its outstanding liability threefold.
terms.whyItMatters: A loyalty-program roleplay asks whether a richer earn rate is affordable, and the answer depends on how much of what is issued is assumed never to be claimed — an assumption that turns into a balance-sheet problem when it is wrong.

terms.definition: The civil standard of proof — the plaintiff wins if the claim is more likely true than not, meaning greater than 50% — which sits far below the criminal beyond-a-reasonable-doubt bar and below the intermediate clear-and-convincing standard used for fraud and punitive damages. That gap is why identical conduct can produce liability in a civil suit and no conviction in a criminal one.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-procedure questions ask why a company can be found liable for fraud after prosecutors declined to bring charges.

terms.definition: A model where reps sell entirely by phone, email and video from one location, never traveling to the customer. A field visit costs roughly five to ten times as much per contact, so firms set a deal-size floor — accounts below it are covered from the desk and only larger ones earn a visit, which is a coverage-cost decision rather than a preference.
terms.whyItMatters: Sales-management items give a cost per contact and an average order size and ask which channel serves an account segment; a territory-planning roleplay is graded on justifying coverage by cost, not by habit.

terms.definition: The five things customers actually grade — reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy and responsiveness. Reliability, meaning the promise was kept, outweighs the other four in most studies while tangibles rank last, so refurbishing the lobby while orders keep arriving late is the classic misallocation of a service budget.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail-image or service-improvement roleplay wants the spend aimed at the heaviest dimension, and naming that ranking is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Production and consumption happen at the same instant with the buyer present, so the employee is part of the product and no defective unit can be caught before a customer receives it; a manufactured good is built, inspected, and warehoused weeks before anyone buys it.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-quality roleplays are scored on front-line hiring and training as quality control, because there is no inspection step to add between production and the customer.

terms.definition: The number-two or number-three firm by share — roughly 30% against a leader's 40% in Kotler's benchmark structure, above a follower's 20% and a nicher's 10% — which attacks the leader or smaller rivals head-on rather than imitating; a firm with the same share that deliberately copies the leader and avoids provoking retaliation is a follower, so the label is set by chosen posture, not by size alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Strategy roleplays that hand you a share table expect the four positions named and the posture defended; calling every non-leader a competitor loses the distinction.

terms.definition: A five-step workplace discipline — sort out what is not needed, set remaining items in fixed marked locations, shine and inspect, standardize the arrangement in writing, and sustain it by audit — where the fifth step is the one that fails and turns the program into a one-time cleanup.
terms.whyItMatters: Safety and efficiency roleplays reward naming a structured method for a cluttered work area rather than saying 'organize it,' and the sustain-by-audit step is the detail that separates a full answer.

terms.definition: Aristotle's rhetorical syllogism, in which one premise is deliberately left unspoken because the audience already believes it and will supply it themselves. 'We should sponsor the tournament - our customers are all high school families' hides the premise that reaching high school families is worth what the sponsorship costs. The unstated premise is where the argument is strongest with a friendly audience and weakest with a hostile one, because attacking what was never said aloud is easier than attacking what was.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items that ask what assumption a memo's recommendation rests on are asking you to recover exactly this missing premise.

terms.definition: Federal coverage of $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category — so a couple's joint account is insured separately from each spouse's individual account, and the cap applies per institution rather than per branch or per account number.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a client asks whether their savings are safe after a bank failure is scored on stating the dollar cap and the per-depositor, per-bank, per-category structure.

terms.definition: A strategy defining the target population, sample size, and selection method.
terms.whyItMatters: A solid plan is what makes research findings trustworthy.

terms.definition: The percentage change in unit sales delivered by a one-percent change in advertising spending — 3% more volume on 10% more spend is 0.3 — and because measured values usually sit near 0.1 to 0.2, doubling the budget rarely comes close to doubling volume; compare it against price elasticity before choosing which lever to pull.
terms.whyItMatters: Budget-allocation items supply both elasticities and expect the higher-return lever chosen with the arithmetic shown; a plan that asks for more advertising without this number has no answer when the judge asks why not a price move instead.

terms.definition: A written brief fixing one campaign's target, its single key benefit claim, the support that proves that claim, the tone of voice and the legal mandatories, so that every execution in every medium argues the same one thing.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on why the pieces of a campaign must agree points here, and a roleplay presenting a campaign is expected to trace each execution back to the one claim the document fixed.

terms.definition: The one person who controls the funds and can release them without another signature, distinct from a technical buyer who screens against specifications and can veto but never approve, and from a user buyer who judges daily impact and lives with the result. Only one of the three can say yes; either of the other two can end the deal.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business items describe three contacts and ask who must be reached before the close; an organizational-selling roleplay is graded on identifying who signs rather than pitching whoever answered the phone.

terms.definition: Scott's grid crossing caring personally with challenging directly: high on both is candor, caring without challenging is ruinous empathy that withholds the correction that would have helped, challenging without caring is obnoxious aggression, and neither is manipulative insincerity. The named failure most managers actually commit is the first, not harshness.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a well-liked employee is quietly underperforming is scored on delivering the specific correction, since softening it to protect the relationship is the graded mistake.

terms.definition: One question rated 1 to 7 on how easy the company made it to get an issue resolved, scored either as the share answering 5 to 7 or as a plain mean. It is asked right after a single service interaction rather than about the relationship, and it predicts repeat purchase better than satisfaction does, because removing effort keeps customers while delight rarely moves them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-redesign roleplay, arguing for deleting steps rather than adding perks needs this metric to carry the recommendation.

terms.definition: The liability booked at the moment of sale for repairs expected later -- units sold times expected claim rate times cost per claim, so 100,000 units at a 2% claim rate and $40 per claim accrues $80,000 of expense in the period the revenue is recognized, not when the repairs happen.
terms.whyItMatters: Questions pairing a generous warranty with its cost are answered with this accrual; a roleplay proposing a longer warranty has to price it, and the reserve is the number to quote.

terms.definition: Optimizes the discounted value of a customer's entire future stream of purchases and will accept a thinner margin on any single sale to protect it, whereas transactional marketing maximizes margin on each separate exchange and budgets acquisition and retention as unrelated lines; the two approaches give opposite answers to whether a long-standing customer should be granted a concession on one order.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a loyal customer asks for an exception is decided by which of the two frames you argue from, and judges expect the alternative named.

terms.definition: A dependency network that estimates each task's expected duration as optimistic plus four times most likely plus pessimistic, divided by six — a weighted three-point estimate for work with uncertain durations, unlike a critical path calculation, which assumes one fixed duration per task.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand you three time estimates for a task and ask for the expected duration; the weighted formula, not a plain average of the three numbers, is the scored answer.

terms.definition: Occurs when short-term Treasury yields sit above long-term ones — the 10-year minus 2-year spread turns negative — because investors expect rate cuts and weaker growth ahead. It has preceded every U.S. recession since the 1950s, typically by six to twenty-four months, which is why it is treated as a leading signal rather than a description of current conditions.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle items that hand you bond yields at several maturities are asking what the shape of the curve forecasts, not what the economy is doing today.

terms.definition: What a deposit actually earns over a year once compounding is counted, which is why a savings account paying 5% compounded monthly returns more than 5%.
terms.whyItMatters: A savings-comparison roleplay hands the competitor two accounts with the same stated rate but different compounding periods; APY is the only figure that ranks them.

terms.definition: Fits the line y = a + bx through the observations so the slope b estimates how much the outcome moves per one-unit change in the driver, letting a finding be stated as each extra $1,000 of local ad spend adding 62 units; a correlation coefficient reports only how tight the relationship is and yields no rate of change to plan with.
terms.whyItMatters: Turning research into a recommendation a manager can budget against needs the slope, which is why forecasting prompts reach for this rather than a correlation.

terms.definition: Carries advertising effect forward as this week's effect = this week's spending effect + (retention rate × last week's carried effect); at a retention rate of 0.7 a flight that ends today still delivers 70% of its pull next week and 49% the week after, which is why a brand can stop spending and not lose sales immediately.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-scheduling questions ask whether a brand can go dark for a month, and this decay arithmetic answers it; it also fixes how long after a campaign ends a plan may still credit sales to that campaign.

terms.definition: A prize promotion whose winners are drawn purely at random, which means it must strip one of the three elements of an illegal lottery — prize, chance and consideration — by publishing a free alternate method of entry so that no purchase is ever necessary.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay client who wants entries limited to paying customers is proposing an illegal lottery without realizing it, and the competitor is scored on naming the three elements and the free-entry fix rather than just calling it risky.

terms.definition: An insider with real political capital who argues the vendor's case in meetings the vendor is not invited to, and whose own standing rises if the purchase works out. A coach, by contrast, supplies intelligence and coaching on how to navigate the account but cannot spend influence or move the decision — access is not the same as power.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business items describe a friendly contact who shares information but has no budget and ask what role that person plays; a long-cycle selling roleplay expects you to test for personal stake, not just friendliness.

terms.definition: The share of respondents picking the top boxes on a satisfaction scale — the 4s and 5s on a 5-point scale, so 380 top-box replies out of 500 is 76%. It measures one transaction immediately after it happens, while the recommend question measures the whole relationship, which is why the two can move in opposite directions in the same month.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items supply raw response counts and expect the top-box percentage; roleplays expect the right survey chosen for a transaction rather than a relationship.

terms.definition: Requires equal pay for men and women performing jobs of equal skill, effort and responsibility under similar working conditions in the same establishment, and unlike a Title VII claim it needs no proof of intent. An employer escapes liability only through one of four defenses — a seniority system, a merit system, a system measuring quantity or quality of production, or any factor other than sex — and may never correct a gap by lowering the higher-paid worker's wage.
terms.whyItMatters: A pay-audit roleplay is scored on naming a permitted defense for the differential rather than asserting that the two jobs simply have different titles.

terms.definition: Unused capacity is destroyed the moment it goes unsold: a 200-room hotel that sells 150 rooms tonight cannot add the other 50 to tomorrow's inventory, which is why capacity is priced by demand period; unsold physical goods simply stay in inventory and sell later.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about slow midweek nights are scored on demand-shifting tactics -- off-peak pricing, overbooking policy -- that follow directly from capacity that cannot be stored.

terms.definition: A brand's own market share divided by the share of its single largest competitor — 20% against a leader's 40% is 0.5x, and only the market leader can score above 1.0 — which is the horizontal axis of the growth-share matrix; two brands holding an identical absolute share therefore land in opposite quadrants depending on how dominant the rival directly above each of them happens to be.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that reports 20% share and calls it strong is answered by asking what the leader holds; the ratio, not the raw percentage, is what drives the portfolio decision.

terms.definition: A horizontal bar timeline showing each task's start, duration and overlap against calendar dates; it displays schedule but not logic, whereas a PERT network draws the dependency arrows that reveal which tasks actually control the finish date.
terms.whyItMatters: Project-management roleplays ask which tool to bring to a status meeting: the bar timeline communicates progress to a client, but it cannot answer which delay pushes the deadline.

terms.definition: The output produced per unit of input, such as per worker or per hour.
terms.whyItMatters: Higher productivity lowers cost and builds competitive advantage.

terms.definition: Concluding that a difference is real when it is not, the false positive that a 0.05 significance threshold knowingly accepts about 5% of the time; the mirror-image mistake of missing a difference that genuinely exists is a Type II error, and tightening the threshold to cut the risk of one necessarily raises the risk of the other.
terms.whyItMatters: Deciding whether a test result justifies a full rollout, the tested judgment is what it costs to be wrong in each direction, not just whether the number cleared 0.05.

terms.definition: A warehouse layout placing one central fact table of numeric measures among denormalized dimension tables, each exactly one join away from the facts; the snowflake variant normalizes those dimensions into further sub-tables, which saves storage and removes redundancy but adds a join to every query that touches them.
terms.whyItMatters: A database-design item shows a sales fact table ringed by product, store and date tables and asks why the dimensions repeat values instead of being split further.

terms.definition: Takes last period's actual as next period's number and nothing else, and exists to be the benchmark: compute its error first, and any model whose MAPE is not meaningfully below that baseline is not paying for the effort it costs, however advanced the technique behind it sounds.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask which forecasting approach a firm should keep; the defensible answer is whichever one beats the zero-effort baseline by a measured margin, and a plan that cannot show that improvement loses the argument for its forecasting spend.

terms.definition: An arrangement where a manufacturer reimburses part of a retailer's local advertising cost, usually on the condition that the ad features the manufacturer's brand and follows its format and logo rules, with reimbursement accrued against the retailer's purchase volume.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail roleplay where the store cannot afford a campaign alone is solved by claiming these funds, and the competitor is expected to name the strings attached rather than treat the money as unrestricted.
